question: Tell me about a time you changed something inside someone else's area.

raiseTranscript.text: I updated the formatting in a shared onboarding doc owned by another new grad on my team. I noticed inconsistencies that were confusing for new hires, so I proposed changes in a comment thread and asked for their input before editing.
They were initially protective but agreed after I showed the data from two recent hires who had questions. We iterated together and I only made the edit once they approved.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you changed something inside someone else's area.
Role: new grad on team, situation: shared onboarding doc had confusing formatting
Actions: posted comment with proposed edits + examples from recent hires, waited for approval
Outcome: doc updated, owner became collaborator on future changes
Quote: 'I only made the edit once they approved.'
Follow-up: What was their reaction? -> showed data, iterated together
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Collaboration. The candidate described editing a shared onboarding document owned by a peer. They posted proposed changes in comments with examples from recent hires and only edited after receiving approval. This shows early awareness of boundaries and basic respect for ownership. The follow-up revealed they used data rather than opinion to build agreement. Biggest strength is the explicit step of waiting for approval instead of assuming permission.

lowerTranscript.text: I just went in and fixed the formatting on a doc another teammate owned because it looked wrong to me.
Did you talk to them first?
Not really, I figured it was obvious. They complained later but the doc was better so it was fine.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you changed something inside someone else's area.
Role: new grad, situation: noticed bad formatting in teammate's doc
Quote: 'They complained later but the doc was better so it was fine.'
Follow-up: Did you talk to them first? -> no, assumed it was obvious
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Collaboration. The candidate edited a teammate-owned document without any prior discussion. When asked, they admitted they did not check first and dismissed the owner's complaint by saying the change was obviously better. This reflects a pattern of acting first and handling relationships second. The core gap is lack of recognition that ownership matters even on small shared items.

raiseTranscript.text: Another team owned the billing retry logic that was causing customer support tickets. I mapped the impact, wrote a one-pager with proposed changes, and scheduled time with their lead to review before touching any code.
They worried about risk. I offered to run a small A/B test in their staging environment and let their on-call own the rollout. We ended up shipping together and support tickets dropped 18%.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you changed something inside someone else's area.
Role: senior engineer, situation: billing retry logic owned by adjacent team causing tickets
Actions: wrote impact one-pager, met with their lead, proposed A/B test they would own
Outcome: joint rollout, 18% drop in tickets
Quote: 'I offered to run a small A/B test in their staging environment and let their on-call own the rollout.'
Follow-up: How did you handle pushback? -> addressed risk concern with test they controlled
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Collaboration. The candidate identified a cross-team issue in billing retries and prepared a one-pager before approaching the owning team. They addressed risk concerns by offering an A/B test that the other team would run and own. This produced a measurable reduction in support tickets. The approach demonstrates influence through preparation and shared ownership rather than unilateral change. Biggest strength is giving the owning team control of the rollout.

lowerTranscript.text: I refactored the retry logic in another team's service because it was inefficient. I sent a PR and tagged them.
What happened with the owning team?
They were annoyed at first and asked for a revert. We eventually merged after some meetings but it took extra work to calm things down.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you changed something inside someone else's area.
Role: senior engineer, situation: inefficient retry logic in another team's service
Actions: refactored and opened PR without prior discussion
Outcome: owning team requested revert, required meetings to resolve
Quote: 'They were annoyed at first and asked for a revert.'
Follow-up: What happened with the owning team? -> extra meetings needed to recover relationship
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Collaboration. The candidate refactored code in another team's service and opened a PR without advance discussion. The owning team reacted negatively and requested a revert, requiring follow-up meetings to repair the relationship. This shows a pattern of prioritizing technical improvement over cross-team coordination. The main gap is treating the PR as sufficient communication instead of securing buy-in first.

raiseTranscript.text: We needed to standardize the incident management tool across three product orgs that each had their own process. I ran a two-week discovery with representatives from each org, surfaced the trade-offs in a leadership forum, and secured agreement on a single tool with a phased migration plan they co-owned.

Some orgs valued deep customization while others wanted simplicity. We chose the simpler tool and gave the customization-heavy orgs extra migration support and a six-month exception window for legacy incidents.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you changed something inside someone else's area.
Role: director/VP, situation: three orgs using different incident tools
Actions: two-week discovery with reps, leadership forum on trade-offs, phased migration co-owned by orgs
Outcome: single tool adopted with exception window for one org
Quote: 'We chose the simpler tool and gave the customization-heavy orgs extra migration support and a six-month exception window.'
Follow-up: What trade-offs did you surface? -> customization vs simplicity, addressed with support and exception
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Collaboration. The candidate drove standardization of an incident tool across three separate organizations by conducting discovery with representatives and presenting trade-offs at a leadership forum. They preserved autonomy for the most affected group through a six-month exception and extra support. This produced org-wide alignment without top-down mandate. Biggest strength is the explicit handling of differing priorities through structured negotiation and phased ownership.

lowerTranscript.text: I decided we should move everyone to one incident tool to reduce costs and just announced the decision in the all-hands.
How did the other orgs respond?
Two orgs pushed back hard and we had to delay the rollout six months while we negotiated exceptions. It created friction that took a while to unwind.

The core gap is relying on announcement instead of early, structured alignment with stakeholders who owned their own processes.
